label: Unstable structure
summary: Buildings damaged by fire, flood, earthquake, storms or years of neglect can drop floors, ceilings, walls and roofs without warning. Collapsed shelving and piled stock can bury you. Getting trapped alone is how people die.
signs: Cracks you can fit a coin edge into, especially diagonal ones from the corners of doors and windows
Doors and windows that jam or have pulled out of square
Sagging, bouncy or bowed floors, ceilings and roofs
Fire damage: charred beams, or crumbling concrete with rusty steel showing
Water damage: stained, soft or rotten floors and ceilings, and mould
Leaning walls, bulging brickwork, fresh dust or creaking
do: Look all the way around the outside before going in
Tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back; go in pairs
Know two ways out before you go deep inside
Test the floor ahead with a pole or bar
Walk close to walls, where floors are best supported
Leave at once if you hear creaking or see fresh dust falling
dont: Don't enter buildings that have burned, flooded or been through an earthquake unless you must
Don't climb on rubble or collapsed stock
Don't pull or cut posts, beams or braces
Don't jump onto floors, or bunch several people on one spot
Don't go into basements under damaged buildings
Don't go in if you smell gas, and don't use flames or flick switches in a damaged building
ppe: Hard hat with the chin strap done up
Boots with toe caps and puncture-resistant soles
An N95 or better against dust; P100 filters if there may be asbestos
firstAid: If someone is trapped, call for help and don't become a second casualty
Free a trapped person as quickly as you safely can, then get medical help
Dust in eyes: rinse with clean water
A head injury with confusion, vomiting or drowsiness needs urgent medical care

Someone pinned under heavy weight for a long time (often an hour or more) can collapse soon after being freed, and their kidneys can fail days later: keep them lying down and watched, and get medical help even if they seem fine
